FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, Oct 2nd.

SEA PLANES WILL SEEK WHALES FOR FLOATING FACTORY
                                          2.10.46.
The United Whalers' 15000-ton factory ship BALAENA, first of
its kind to be fitted with aircraft for whale-spotting and
weather reconnaissance, has been handed over to her owners
after trials in Belfast Lough, and will shortly leave for
the Antarctic in search of badly needed whale oil.
The ship will carry three converted Walrus amphibian air-
craft which will be launched from a double-acting catapult
working on a cordite charge, or lowered over the side for a
normal take-off by the crane which also lifts them from the
water after a flight.
The BALAENA will act as mother ship for a fleet of about ten
whale-catchers, and her factory contains one of the largest
oil-producing plants ever installed in a ship, and elaborate
machinery for dealing with by-products; refrigerating gear
will freeze the choicest parts of the whale meat for human
consumption.   The picture shows
A close-view of the stern and flight-deck of the
BALAENA, showing one of the amphibian Walruses and the
crane, and the aperture through which the whales are
hauled up into the factory.

1,000,000, EELS.
LIVE IN A BARGE FULL OF HOLES          DG/FM

Believed to be the first of its kind ever to
be built in this country, and certainly the
first of this particular design, the eel barge
"Johan", is literally a ship full of holes.
The centre part of the barge is perforated so that
water can be allowed to flow freely into it.
Watertight compartments support the barge, fore and
aft, and the deck is no more than 18 inches above
water level. The owner is Mr H. G. Kuitjen,
an importer of live eels. The eels come from
the seas between Norway and Corsica, and they are
brought by boat from the Continent.
The eels usually arrive in the autumn and are
graded by size into separate compartments. From
the barge they are packed into wet boxes for
Billingsgate. It is estimated that the barge
will 120,000 lbs of live eels- the shipping of
this 50 ton cargo will not increase the draught
draught of the vessel as the cargo is waterborne.

PHOTO SHOWS:- The graded eels are transferred into
floating containers alongside the barge at Heybridge
Basin, Malden, Essex. These are also floating
perforated containers.

Goodbye,
old friend!
WHEN summer comes, and
the green rows of sugar-
beet glisten in the sun,
we shall miss Old Captain.
For it has been Sam's custom
for many years, on mornings when
butterflies have danced and the
cuckoo's call has sounded over the
fields, to go into the stable and
say to the boy George: "Horse-
hoeing—we'll take Captain."
He was the obvious choice. No
other horse could do it so well.
Ever since he was first broken-in
as a colt, horse-hoeing has been
his job on the farm.
It meant walking steadily and
carefully between the rows, up and
down the field, up and down, hour
after hour, in the heat of the sun.
It was irksome, monotonous work.
But it was work that, done well,
added tons to the crop.
Captain—the willing horse—did
it always. And in the intervals
between one long horse-hoeing
season and another he did odd
jobs of carting mangolds and
muck and straw and water with a
stolid patience that earned him
the reputation of being the most
reliable old plodder we have ever
had on this farm.
"He was a kind ole hoss," says
Sam.
---

less in the horseyard, with
his head lowered almost to

THEY SWEAT FOR BRITAIN. 				E.M./RS.

Men now working in the great foundries of the Ministry of
Supply are going at overpowering pressure to supply, not
only our Army with all the modern weapons to beat the 'Hun',
but more and more tanks and guns for Russia.  Before going
into these great factories, many of the men were clerks,
motor-drivers, horse dealers, roundsmen, etc., jobs which
are far removed from their present employment, but, as can
be seen from these pictures, this is no handicap to them
and they are putting every effort into their new tasks.

Photo shows:-  Mr. Woolston, who, before the war was a
heavy timber carrier, makes light work of his new job
and enjoys the joke as he wrings the sweat from his vest
after a day's work.

BACK-YARD BOAT-BUILDERS PLAN TO SAIL TO AUSTRALIA D/HA

Neighbours of Mr and Mrs P.J. Munro of Oxberry Avenue,
Fulham, can seen ship-building in progress from their
back windows. Mr. Munro, production manager of cosmetics
with a West End hairdresser, is at present building a

worker, Mr. H. Woodbridge, and he and his wife hope to
sail to Australia. Their only experience of sailing so
far has been on the Norfolk Broads, and Mr. Munro has
been building the £500 boat from library books. When
finished the craft will be lifted into the lane at the
back, and taken to Putney where it will be launched,

title: A photographic print of Home & Housing, Pre War Only, Housing - Slums - London Only
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Home + Housing Â» Pre War Only Â» Housing - Slums - London Only.
gem_transcription_flat:
Housing (Post-War) F192 D3 Slums.
---
1983-5236/49161
---
PROBLEM OF A WOMAN AND SIX CHILDREN
---
Living in one room - a wooden fruit picker's
hut, on Wested Farm, Crockenhill, near Swanley,
Kent, is Mrs. May Cropp, her three children and a
further three granchildren (offspring of one of her
daughters).
She is a squatter. There is no sanitation
anywhere near the hut - nor the usual amenities. The
hut leaks, is unsanitary, and is certainly not
weatherproof.
How she came to be there does not matter - what
does matter is that she cannot get another home to
live - and owing to the bad state of affairs the
farmer, C.T. Miller, of Wested Farm, has asked the
police to evict them in the hope that they will
be found better accomodation.
As it is, the children - ranging from a few
months to six years - cannot possibly be properly
fed, clothed and educated - and there is no talk of
them going regularly to school.
In this cold weather, some of them are to
be seen playing in the mud around their "home".
The Dartford Rural District Council, under
whose jurisdiction their "home" comes, should look
into the matter - the farmer is certainly not to
blame - it is the best housing he can offer - even
to squatters.
PICTURE SHOWS:

1. Mrs. May Cropp with her three children
and granchildren in their one roomed hut.

19835 4/12/46 John Topham, Sidcup, Kent.
---
Fil Housing P.W. Slums.
XR Dartford
XR Personal
See also G.D. WALLACE MP
---

BUILDING UP OUR TIMBER STOCKS.        MJH/HT

During the two World Wars, our woodlands were
seriously denuded of timber. Today, the Forestry
Commission and private woodland owners are pressing
ahead with the vital task of forming new forests and
re-stocking the old. The year 1956 has marked a milestone
in the history of the Forestry Commission, for it has
seen the planting by the Commission of the one
millionth acre of new woodland. Thus the area of woodland
planted to date by the Commission is more than 1,500
square miles - an area larger than Kent, nearly
twice the extent of Glamorgan and nearly two-thirds
of Perthshire. This million acres is made up of some
500 forests, which are well distributed over the length
and breadth of Britain. In recent years, well over
100-million trees - including more than 10 million hardwoods -
have been planted annually by the Commission and many of
the forests are now producing timber in substantial
quantities; in 1955, the total production amounted to
600,000 tons. Today there is hardly a county without
a national forest and scenes such as these, in the
Commission's Rendlesham Forest in East Anglia, are typical
of what is to be seen in many other parts of the country.


PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: "Timber" and the fellers
crouch as a pine comes crashing down in
Rendlesham Forest (Suffolk).

A new Husband for "Moina".
The Belgian Government have presented the London
Zoo with a new husband for "Moina". He isn't
old enough or big enough to go with her yet,
as he is only about a year old. "Meng" as he
is called after the village where he was found,

the Mountain or Kivu race of Gorilla. When he
grows up he will be almost twice the size of
the late lamented "Mok". Male Kivu Gorillas

the baby Chimpanzee at the Zoo which has been

can be penetrated by a bullet, also the splintered wood
carried away by the bullet can produce nasty wounds.
The present suggestion is to pre-cast the embrasure
opening of the desired aperture and angle, the outer
extremity having a light sheet steel framing embedded
in the face to prevent the concrete edges shattered by
a bullet from being detached and forming missiles.
The embrasure weighs less than 1½ cwt. and can easily
be lifted into place by two men.  Manufacture can be
made in quite simple wooden moulds by any local building
contractor, breeze block manufacturer, in Corporation
yards, and so on; using the quick setting concrete
and be produced ready for installation within 24 hours.

THE pit where 45 men
are trapped behind a
wall of flame became an
almost-certain grave last
night. Rescuers had
found a pocket of deadly
carbon monoxide gas
spreading through the
shaft where the men were
caught.
The gas—miners call it
"White Damp"—is caused
by the fire as it rages through
the pit workings at Auchen-
geich Colliery, at Chryston,
near Glasgow.
It can kill in a short time.
The men were trapped in the
shaft as they rode from the pit
bottom to the coal face on a
bogie train.
Heavy
Last night, more than 12
hours after the outbreak, res-
cuers were still trying to reach
the train in a haulage way,
1,050 feet down.
One of them said as he came
to the surface: "Anyone in that
part of the haulage way is dead.
"The whole place is alight,
glowing red and as hot as a coke
oven. Every scrap of timber is
on fire. Identification of many
of the bodies may be very
difficult."
And a Coal Board statement
said: "It is feared that a heavy
loss of life must be expected."
The fire started in a fan about
a mile from the coalface. Smoke
spread quickly along a parallel
shaft used as a return airway.
The men on the train were
trapped in the smoke. They
signalled for the train to be
returned to the pit bottom they
had just left.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, June 25th.
PROGRESS ON BRITAIN'S AERIAL GIANT
25.6.47.
At the Bristol Aeroplane Works at FILTON, progress is being
made on the huge 125-ton "Brabazon I" landplane - the largest
ever to be built in Britain - which when completed will carry
100 people direct from London to New York. A special runway,
for which a complete village had to be demolished and which
will cost £2,000,000, and an assembly hall, are being con-
structed to get this giant into the air. She will have a wing-
span of 230 ft (30ft longer than between the main structures
of Tower Bridge), and will be powered by eight Centaurus gas-
turbines of 2500 h.p. each. The picture shows -
A general view of the huge machine under construction in the
Bristol workshops. The giant fuselage and centre sections of
the wings are supported by cradles and scaffolding, while in the
foreground one of the massive outer wings is being erected.
The aircraft is being constructed in portions, which will
later be moved to the giant assembly hall for the final
assembly.

MAKING NEW RIGGING FOR NELSON'S FLAGSHIP "VICTORY"

A team of men and women have started work at Chatham 
to make a complete new rigging for Nelson's Flagship, 
VICTORY". They are working in the same timber-built 
rope "walks" used by the men who refitted Victory for 
Trafalgar after she had been for five years in the 
Medway as a prison hospital ship. The work is being 
carried out at Chatham's Ropery - the Admiralty's only 
rope-making establishment. Methods of making the rope 
are almost the same as in the days of Nelson except 
that women are employed in some of the operations, 
now done by machines.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Sport, Cricket
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Sport Â» Cricket.
gem_transcription_flat:
DAILY
17 JAN 1962
HERALD
---
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
17 JAN 1962
RETURN
ART LIBRARY
---
On the ball as usual—Craftsman Ken Jeffrey
Strike? They’ll all
play it straight
A STEADY stitcher is
this chap, 50-year-old
Ken Jeffrey. And yester-
day he stitched on as care-
fully as usual—unworried
by the dispute in his little
industry.
He is one of the men
demanding a pay rise for
their very special craft—
making cricket balls by
hand.
The men are expected to
stage Britain's friendliest
walk-out in nine days.
Employees and workers
are prepared for a long
spell of stone-walling.
Both sides are determined
that the affair—their first
major wage disagreement
in 30 years—should be
managed cordially.
NO CHANGE
In the smal family firms
—all in Kent—that make
up the country's cricket-
ball industry the works
manager is just "one of
the chaps." And no-one is
quite sure about strike
rules anyway.
Eight-five ball makers at
three Tonbridge firms and
35 at Teston, near Maid-
stone, are involved. So are
36 bat makers at Roberts-
bridge, Sussex.
They want a rise which
would add about 25s. a
week to their pay packets,
which range from £9 to
£16.
At the two-storey
Lillywhite Frowd factory
at Tonbridge, works man-
ager John Dyer said
yesterday: "We’re a happy
bunch here and the strike
won’t change a thing."
"If the chaps do walk
out I'll be drinking in the
pub with them just the
same."
'KNOCK 'EM'
But he added: "I don't
agree with them. A pay
rise would kill the industry
with the cut price compe-
tition from machine-made
cricket balls from Aus-
tralia, Pakistan and
India."
Mr. Roy Thomas, branch
secretary of the National
Union of Furniture Trade
Operatives (Cricket Ball
Section) works at the fac-
tory as a closer—shaping
cricket ball covers.
"We'll knock them for
six," he said. "We’re badly
done by compared with
workers in other indus-
tries.
"But there will be no
animosity. We can get
through this spot of bother
without falling out."
---
KEN JEFFREY
---
1962 - 107 - 27
---
Indus Sport Cricket
---
P. 9. 2 11/12 d x 6'' deel
---

Roe, Princess class, 140-ton flying-boats, known as the

FROM LEICESTER TO LONDON -- PULLING
ELECRICALLY DRIVEN DELIVERY VAN.

IVOR JONES, 24, of Leicester, believed
he was the most unique of Saturday's walkers.
He set out from Leicester at 1.30 p.m. on Friday
pulling an electrically driven delivery van. Twenty-
four hours later he was at [crossed out] Markyate, near
Dunstable, 30 miles from his objective, Marble Arch.
"This is the first and last time I shall do anything
like this and I am only doing it now because a friend
bet me a fiver I couldn't make it", he said. Ivor,
who was listening to the efforts of the other walkers
on a radio strapped to the top of the van, added:
"I know this will not be any record time but I can't
go any faster as every 17 miles I have to stop for
half-an-hour while the van's batteries are re-charged.
"I have had no training, but so far I've not got any
blisters. My only discomforture is that I have
caught a cold".
KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- IVOR JONES pictured
passing through Dunstable today.

ONE OF THE OLDEST OF FARMING ARTS.              AW/RS

58-year-old Mr. Tom Allen Hancock, a smallholder at
Brook, Kent, is one of the few remaining exponents of
the thousands of years old art of flail-threshing.
The flail he uses was used by his father and his
grandfather before him and is nearly 150 years old.
It consists of a club swinging by a leather thong
from the end of a 5 ft pole; the pole is held in both
hands and the club swung to beat the sheaves of corn
laid out on the barn floor. Tom still relies on it
for threshing peas and beans.  He can remember the
days when his family had six men in the barn working
flails - keeping them occupied most of the winter.

Photo shows:-   Mr. Hancock threshing with his ancient
flail.

GREAVES.  D.H.  23rd. 10. 44.

Mr. and Mrs. John Green and their family are the
first to occupy a pre-fabricated hut house in Poplar.
10.000 of these hut homes are to be built in London.
Here are the Green family photographed round the
fireside of their new home in Glengall road, Poplar
tonight. L.-R. John, aged 7. Mrs. Green and
Christine, aged 3. Mr. Green. Margaret, aged 11. holding
Peter the family pet.
---
GREAVES
---
m7660.
---
F192 / 3D HOUSING POST-WAR / EARLY POST WAR DIFFICULTIES / HOUSES/TEMPORARY PRE-FABS
---
DDA 708
---
POST WAR PRE FABS
---
AS the hands of the clock
pointed to six last night
three-year-old Christine
nodded in her chair before
the fire.
In a sleepy voice she said:
"Mummy, I want to go to my
cot."
These eight words told how
life has changed for Mr. and
Mrs. John Green and their
family of three.
Every night for the past five
months when Christine
wanted to go to bed, Mrs.
Green carried her out into
the garden from a bomb-
blasted kitchen to put her on
a bunk in a damp Anderson
shelter.
John, aged seven, and
Margaret, aged 11, followed
behind.
Mrs. Green went back to sleep
in a chair while her husband
slept on the floor. The back
kitchen was all the accommoda-
tion the fly-bombs had left them.
There was no room for them
to sit around the table for a
meal.
Yesterday the Green family
moved 200 yards down Glengall-
grove, Cubitt Town, Poplar, to
start a new life in a new home.
They are the first tenants of
Poplar's first hut-homes. Ten
thousand of them have been
promised as a temporary relief
for London's housing shortage.
It is not palatial; yet to Mrs.
Green it is a palace.
There are two bedrooms,
living-room and a partitioned-off
kitchenette.
Mrs. Green talked of the new
home.
"Think what it means to have
an electric cooker and to have
them all round the table for
proper meals; to have a nice
clean sink and good food cup-
boards and decent beds.
"I never gave up, and I always
managed to cook meals some-
how—but this is wonderful."

By PETER BATT
A 13-YEAR-OLD boy clung to life by
his fingertips yesterday—130ft. high
on the famous Kennington Oval gaso-
meter.
Special constable John Laurance, aged 30,
inched his way along the topmost girder
and grasped the boy's hand. "Steady lad,"
he coaxed softly. "Hang on."
But the sobbing boy told him: "I'm tired.
I want to let go." And slumped unconscious.
The gasometer that loomed
over so many Test matches had
never known drama like this..
watched by hundreds in the
street below.
Hung on
For 30 nightmare minutes
Mr. Laurance hung on to the
boy's hand.
It slipped slowly from his
grasp, almost down to the finger-
tips. Then firemen reached
them.
They shouted to Mr. Laurance
to secure the boy to a girder by
tying a flagpole rope round him.
He then hung precariously,
clasping the boy's arm round a
girder as his other hand tied
the rope.
Firemen gently lowered the
boy in a bo'sun's chair. Mr.
Laurance climbed down a cat-
walk—and went home.
Said Thomas Spiers, a gas-
ometer workman: "Mr. Laur-
ance is the bravest man I've
ever seen. I couldn't have done
that for a million pounds."
Mr. Laurence, attached to
Bow-street police station, was
off duty when he saw the boy
hanging on high above.
Last night the police returned
the boy to an institution from
which he had escaped.
Rescue point—where the boy
clung to life.
---

- 4 OCT 1962

title: A photographic print of Industry, Fuel & Power - Coal, Accidents, Cambrian Colliery Rhondda, May 1965
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Fuel + Power - Coal Â» Accidents Â» Cambrian Colliery Rhondda, May 1965.
gem_transcription_flat:
Indus-Fuel & Power-Coal- Accidents- Cambrian Colliery, Rhonnda. May 1965
---
IN the Valley of Sorrow hundreds stood in silence last night to hear 31 names read out. This was the formal, official end to a day of tragedy.
Under sodium lights in Clydach Vale, the grim-faced Rhondda. The people gathered. The bereaved wives, mothers and children.
In the nearby Assembly Hall workmen who were still thinking: "It could have been us."
From a police car the loudspeaker drifted out, read by Glamorgan's Chief Constable, Mr. Melbourne
Last of all came the names of the dead rolled out, by the colliery manager, 42-year-old Ernest Breeze, and u n d e r - m a n a g e r Leslie Williams.
A GASP
A final gasp went up from the crowd. Mr. Thomas told them it would be as well if the list would be posted up for inspection.
"Perhaps he said, gently: "Then it would be as well to disperse to your homes." Reluctantly the people drifted home to ponder on the lovely little cul-de-sac of the Rhondda Valley.
In Clydach Vale today, the front doors are all open. Some women stand at their front gates, a few are still at the pithead.
There is no hope left—and no doubt.
All the dead miners have been identified by the numbers on their lamps. Nobody is unaccounted for.
The explosion was in the colliery's No. 1 pit — an up-to-date section of the colliery.
Thirty-one men in the immediate area of the blast were killed instantly.
WAS IT GAS?
How did it happen? It is possible gas seeped through from an old disused working at the weekend. An official inquiry will find the facts. The horror of it all. The Black Hell, as some miners called it—without trying to dramatise.
The victims were working 850ft. underground two and a half miles from the pit-head. They were in a tunnel only 2ft. 8in. high.
Rescue workers went down after the blast. But hope was never really there.
A worker who joined the rescue, his s h a k e n grey-faced, said: "The sight was terrible."
Some men were decapitated. Others without arms and legs. Their clothing was ripped to shreds.

            A NEW TANKER JETTY FOR SCOTLAND      6.9.57

The first steel piles have been driven for a new tanker
jetty that is being built for British Petroleum Ltd. at
Finnart, on Loch Long, Scotland. When it is completed
in 1958, the jetty will accommodate the largest tankers.
The new jetty, which is about half a mile south of B.P.'s
present tanker jetty and installation, will have two concrete
decked shore arms each 180ft long. One arm will carry a
roadway for light vehicles and the other a pipe-track. The
jetty head, at which there will be a low water depth of
55 ft, will be 320 feet long.
Tankers will be able to         discharge up to 6,000 tons
an hour of crude oil         through two 24 inch pipelines
connecting with four new storage tanks now being built.
and the four tanks at the present installation. All these
tanks will be linked through the existing pumphouse
to the 57 miles pipeline to B.P.'s Grangemouth Refinery
on the Firth of Forth.
It was announced earlier this year that the annual
processing capacity of Grangemouth Refinery is to be
raised from 2,200,000 tons to 3,100,000 tons, This increased
capacity will be close to the annual carrying capacity
of the Finnart pipeline.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Fuel & Power, Oil & Petrol - from Coal
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Fuel + Power Â» Oil + Petrol - from Coal.
gem_transcription_flat:
PETROL FROM COAL:  HOW PROCESS WORKS.
---
1983-5236/51528
---
KEY TO WORKING MODEL.

      The model is intended to show, in simplest form, the main features of a
plant hydrogenating coal to make motor spirit.  It is not intended to 
represent closely either the Billingham plant itself or the entire process
as operated commercially.  For the sake of simplicity, the process is 
represented as being carried out in one stage in place of the three actually
employed, and many details, such as heat exchanges, are omitted entirely.

      Clean coal is fed into the hopper (A) and taken by conveyor (B) to storage bunkers (C).  The coal is then
fed to the grinding mills (D), where it is mixed with heavy oil, returned (along a pipe S) from a subsequent
stage of the process, and the whole ground into a fine paste consisting of 50% of coal and 50% of oil.

      High pressure paste injectors, (E), force this paste against a pressure of 3700 lbs. per square inch
(250 atmospheres) into the converter system, and at this point it joins the hydrogen, which has been manu-
factured, purified and compressed in the plant (P).  The two are heated together in the preheater (F) to the
reaction temperature of 450ºC.  The reaction takes place in the special heavy steel forging, or converter (G).
Most of the products and gas pass overhead from the converter through a cooler (H) to a catchpot (I) where the
condensed mixed oils separate from the uncondensed gases.  The former are collected in a tank (J) and pumped,
(K), to a distillation unit where they are heated in the furnace, (L), and fractionated in a column, (M).
Petrol is distilled off, is condensed in a cooler (N) and, after very limited refining, stored in tanks (O),
ready for shipment in tankers or rail cars.

      The heavy fractions (S) are returned to the process, part being used as pasting oil in the coal mills, (D)
and the remainder hydrogenated further so that only petrol is finally produced.

      Going back to the converter (G), a heavy residual sludge including all the coal ash is purged off the
bottom of the system and passed to a sludge plant (R), where as much oil is recovered as possible and the
remainder made into solid fuel for burning under boilers.

      The uncondensed gases separated in the catchpot vessel (I) are treated to recover all the available
hydrogen and the balance, consisting chiefly of hydrocarbon gas, returned to the hydrogen plant (P) as a source
of further hydrogen for use in the process.

CARRYING ON A FAMOUS NAME
            24.7.38.
World-wide interest has been evoked in the forthcoming launch
of the new Cunard-White Star liner "MARETANIA" from Cammell-
Laird's Yard at Birkenhead. The ceremony, which is to be
broadcast, is to be performed by LADY BATES on Thursday next,
and all work will be stopped in the yard for 3 hours.       The
vessel perpetuates a name so renowned in the North Atlantic
service, and she will be the biggest liner ever launched in
England. The launch is expected to be very spectacular as she
will take the water without drag chains. It has been estimated
that about 150,000 people will have taken some part in her
construction by the time she is put into service.
   The picture shows a view of the bows as she appears on the
stocks ready for launching, and revealed for the first
time.
FOR PUBLICATION ON MONDAY, JULY 25th.

119, Fleet Street LONDON E.C 4

The eggs and I: Champion layer '808', preening itself over an average year's output. Pic

COUNT them if you like. There are 260—representing the annual output of one rather small chicken.
Since this is at least 20 a year more than any other variety of hen can be expected to produce, Thornbers, the Yorkshire firm who bred it, are understandably jubilant.
It eats, they announce, a mere three and a half ounces of food a day—an ounce less than its competitors — and, in spite of this, more than 85 per cent. of its eggs
[line cut off] n be classified as large.
[line cut off] ey are also reluctant to give precise details of their super-hen's family tree. Understandably, they want to preserve exclusive rights to the bird.
They admit that it took 12 years of research to produce, involved 1,200,000 separate calculations on a computer and has inherited the selected virtues of four different breeds. But further than that the breeders will not go. Just call it "808," they say darkly.
There is only one snag about "808" (it is too skinny to make good eating, but that is irrelevant as well as ungrateful). Its 260 eggs a year are all white, which will be sad news for all those people who believe, against all the evidence, that brown eggs taste better.
The breeders are a bit sad about those people, but think they have something for them, too. Their computer has been at it again and they have bred a bird with an annual output of only 240 eggs—but every one of them brown.
It looks as if they are on to another good thing. Not quite as good as "808," perhaps. That could be why they have called this one "404."

gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/42970
---
PITHEAD SHALE FOR SITE OF NEW HOVERPORT.

Lorries loading shale at Chislet colliery, Kent, for the 10 mile
journey to Pegwell Bay, where it will be used in the construction of the
new international hoverport. Half of Chislet's north west tip (about 180,000
cubic yards) is being removed to form the base for the 12-acre landing and
launching pad.

Both black and red shales, which conform to Ministry of Transport
specifications for general fill, are obtainable from colliery sites. The
red shale - which has been used extensively for road making - is becoming
scarce but the black shales of the type used at Pegwell Bay are in
plentiful supply.

The National Coal Board sell shale from site and contractors are
responsible for collection. Contractors operating on colliery sites have
to conform with Board regulations regarding work on tips, but the Board
will advise on methods of working.

More than 6 million tons of shale was sold from pithead sites last
year and the demand is increasing. A small section dealing with sales has
been set up under Mr. N. Little, Marketing Department, National Coal Board,
Hobart House, Grosvenor Place, London, S.W.1.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Scientific Experiments, Binocular, Compass, etc
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Scientific Experiments Â» Binocular, Compass, etc.
gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/56984
---
THE jobs that girls are doing in the marine instruments trade must be making many an old salt quite dizzy turning in his grave. But he can rest in peace. The girls are fully conscious of their great responsibility.
They know that on the little pieces of mica or metal in their hands rest the fate of brave men. Many of them have brothers and husbands in the Merchant Navy, the Royal Navy, the R.A.F., whose lives depend on those very instruments they are making.
Advance is the keynote of the trade; advance in production and design. But progress must go hand in hand with precision. The making of marine instruments seems to run in families.
The trade has been handed down from father to son and through the centuries famous ships have carried instruments designed and produced by familiar names. Today it still goes on, but now instruments in planes as well as ships carry their names. Sextants and compasses are as important in the air as on the sea.
In the workshops one comes across these family traditions.
"That was my baby for fifteen years," says the foreman of the sextant shop, for instance, pointing at the Swiss dividing machine, cutting the degree rack round the arc of a sextant with the precision of 1/1,000th of an inch, and operated by a girl hardly over school age.
He means the machine. But the operator was his "baby" too. She is his seventeen-year-old daughter who has taken over the job which was once her father's. Her grandfather also works in the factory. And his father was in the trade before him. In his day sextants were made of ebony.
War has brought a lot of new blood into the industry. Many more women have been taken on,
---
SAIDMAN

E.M./HT.

PEAT INDUSTRY SWINGS INTO WAR PRODUCTION.

The peat industry has come into its own again in Somerset
where, apart from a small percentage used as fuel by consumers
who collect their own, a greater part of the output is utilised
in the construction of runways on aerodromes - also in the
agricultural world as a fertiliser and dressing.  Transport
difficulties prohibit the use of peat for fuel consumption in
the homes of Britain but Peat has been found to contain many
by-products.  It is used in the making of paper, as insulating
material for rendering buildings soundproof and also in the pro-
duction of alcohol.

Photo shows:-  Women at work stacking cut peat.  On the left
is the higher section known as the "aisle", the water course
called the "baler pit" runs through the centre and the women
on the right are working on the "low".
FOX.    30th October, 1942.                      282442.

XHN)				BORING TWO MILES FOR OIL

Hundreds of men are now hard at work on the slopes of
Portsdown Hill, near Portsmouth, preparing for the
gigantic task of penetrating twice as far beneath
the surface of England as ever before. In this
peaceful spot engineers are making ready to drill to
a point 10,000 feet - or nearly two miles - under the
ground in a search for oil. The hole is to be drilled
with the most modern of machinery, the work being
carried out under the supervision of expert mining
engineers who have been brought from the oilfields of
Persia. Portsdown Hill was decided on as the site
for boring after a careful survey by geologists.

Photo shows:- Workmen under the 136ft. derrick at
Portsdown Hill, where boring will begin.

British and French guns on Tower Hill, outside the
Tower of London, all of which are over 100 years old,
are to be broken up for scrap. Yesterday eight of the

marking corners will be left. Eight guns inside the

will soon be removed by scrap merchants. The guns
will produce about 150 tons of metal.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Boot & Shoe
description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Boot + Shoe.
gem_transcription_flat:
1983-5236/46477
---
INDUSTRY - BOOT & SHOE.
---
ALAN SHARPE, freelance journalist of 31 Richmond Road, Coulsdon,
Surrey has won the top award in the open photo contest - theme
'People at work and play - organised by the London Trades Council in
connection with London 1961 T.U. Festival Week (May 24 - 31).

His winning study of a Mitcham shoe repairer - for over 50 years
a well loved 'character' in his shop opposite the parish cemetary -
is a fine story-telling photograph. It was taken with a 9cm x 12cm
press camera on an Ilford HP3 plate.

Mr. Sharpe, who is a married man with three sons, is secretary
of a 450-strong freelance branch of the N.U.J. and has for many years
been most active in T.U. work, serving on several N.U.J. committees,
and acting as delegate to important Union conferences.

His interest in photography goes back to schooldays. His first
camera - a Kodak box camera - was confiscated at school because Mr.
Sharpe was discovered developing films in an out-of-bounds cellar.

THATCHING MACHINE HELPS ON THE FARM.             E.M./HT.

A machine invented and patented nearly half-a-century ago,
but never used, is now helping to solve labour problems on
British farms. It makes thatches for ricks at half the
cost and in a fifth of the time of the old hand method.
The matting can be made at any time by this machine and
can be stored in rolls till harvest time, so that ricks
can be immediately thatched to cut out risk of damage by
weather. These pictures, taken in Surrey, show the new
thatching machine in use.

Photo shows:- A general view of the thatch making in
progress with a team of four girls.

---
WASTE WOOD SAVES DOLLARS
-- NEW BRITISH INVENTION WILL REVOLUTIONISE THE WORLD'S
INDUSTRIES

All over the country, Britain's industries are geared up
to full production in an all-out effort to supply
the world's markets with the goods they require. During
the making of the goods, much precious material has to
be thrown away as waste - especially wood, which is used
in many industries. As nearly 40% of all wood cut is
lost for productive purposes, this problem has become
a major headache, but due to a new process, this waste
is now being made into "man-made" timber, and promises
to save countless precious dollars in the future. This
new process, known as "Plimber" is a synthetic plastic
timber. The waste wood is pulverised, mixed with other
ingredients, plasticised with artificial resins, subjected
to pressure, and finally cured to produce sheets of man-
made" timber. Plimber, which has the blessing of the Ministry
of Works, causes no new worries for the carpenter, one of
its chief advantages being that it can be worked easily
with ordinary tools.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:- The filled mould goes into the press.
This specially designed hydraulic press is the largest
welded structure of its type in Britain. A few minutes
in the press is all that is required to make firm
boarding. The mould is removed and locked after pressing
in order to retain pressure for some time - until
chemical action is concluded.

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Fuel + Power Â» Oil + Petrol - Oil From The Sea Bed Miscellaneous.
gem_transcription_flat:
Indus.. Oil Misc.
---
THIRTY men escaped death four times yester-
day as a giant runaway oil rig was swept
by a 60 mph. gale towards the open sea.
And inland, hundreds of power-station workers
escaped when three 350ft. cooling towers were
blown to the ground. The men were on their tea-
break at the time.
These were two of the dramas of yesterday's great
gales—gales that killed six people and injured several
others. Near-hurricane winds with gusts of up to
100 mph. swept across the country.
And the luckiest men
alive today are the 30
workers aboard the £2 1/4-
million oil rig Ocean
Prince which snapped a
dozen steel hawsers at
Middlesbrough, Yorkshire,
and floated into the River
Tees before dawn yester-
day.
Four times the men
escaped death.
Escape No. 1 came when the
rig crashed into the side of a
tanker discharging oil.
Escape No. 2 came a quarter
of a mile downstream when the
pre-dawn skies were streaked
with power flashes as the rig's
crane sliced through two power
cables strung across the river.
GELIGNITE
Escape No. 3 happened as the
rig bore down on a tiny dredger
in the river. Aboard the
dredger were 2,000lb. of gelig-
nite—but the dredger crew
towed it to safety and then
took to their boats to escape.
Finally came:
Escape No. 4, when the oil rig
bit deep into a mudbank with-
in sight of the open sea and
almost capsized.
After the men had been taken
off by launches, they sipped tea
and told of their escapes.
Labourer Tom Bradley was
stranded 160 feet up on the rig's
-crane when the Ocean Prince
broke loose.
He said: "Our hearts were in
our mouths as we swept across
the river and ran into the oil
tanker. Fortunately it lurched
but if we had hit it solidly we
might all have been flung over-
board.
"All of us knew of the power
cables over the river, and we
got as low on the rig as we
could. Then we waited for the
sparks to fly . . .
---
5 1/2 " wide x 1 3/4 " deep
---

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S DAILIES.......NOV.26th '56.
SEARCHING FOR OIL IN BRITISH WATERS.
26.11.56.
The first water-borne geophysical survey to be carried
out by The British Petroleum Company off the British Coast
took place recently, in the 1000 ton converted corvette
"SEISLIM", the first British-owned vessel to be specially
equipped for this work, off Swanage and Lulworth Cove.
The purpose was to investigate the nature of the rocks beneath
the sea bed at 10,000 ft. B.P. has been carrying out
a search for oil-bearing rock formations in the British Isles
for the past 21 years and this was its latest effort.
Charges were exploded four and a half feet below the surface
of the water, along a previous plotted line. Vibrations
transmitted into the sea bed and reflected back from various
rock formations were picked up by detectors towed behind
the ship. They were then recorded electrically on a time
chart which is afterwards analysed by experts at The
British Petroleum Company's London office.
Picture shows-

gem_transcription_flat:
1983 - 5236/50000
---
40 BRITISH FAMILIES NOW IN CAMP INTENDED FOR POLIS AND ITALIAN WIVES.

More than 40 families, harassed by Britain's housing shortage,
have now moved into the empty ex United States Army camp at
Chalfont St. Giles, Buckinghamshire.  The camp, estimated to
have cost £500,000, was recently redecorated to house Polish
troops from Italy and their Italian wives.
It is of brick-built huts with hot and cold water, sanitation,
lighting, heating and concrete roads.  It had been empty
for months.
A number of ex Servicemen are among the squatters.
Because they expect visits from police and military authorities,
the new tenants are appointing a committee to resist all
attempts at eviction.  But the War Office has 'no comment
to make' so far.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Inside one of the Army hut homes.  Mrs. Bailey
finishes her toilet while her husband, ex Commando William Bailey,
recently returned from the Far East and China, attends to the stove.
ES August 12th 1946 PN.r.

QUEENIE'S GOT A 'CRUSH' ON THIS JOB.

The 'daily round' is more than
a catch phrase to Queenie, a
West Country mare who has reached
the ripe old age of 30 years.
Queenie has been brought from
retirement to operate the century-
old apple crusher used in
cider-making by Mr. L. Steel of
Church End, Slimbridge,
Gloucestershire.
Hitched to a heavy stone
wheel, Queenie plods round and
round crushing the apples in
the press, believed to be the
last of its type used in the West
Country and one of the very few
left in all Britain.
This year, Mr. Steel hopes to
produce 750 gallons of cider from
apples picked in his own orchards.
PICTURE SHOWS: Queenie operates
the apple crusher. Mr. L. Steel
and an assistant are levelling
apples in the trough.

THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY
GK/7262. Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co. of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest". Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory. They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets. The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it. It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

BANKSIDE POWER STATION STARTS PRODUCTION.

London: A battery of 12 oil-burning boilers at
the new and controversial Bankside Power Station,
at which the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator,
of about 80,000 horse-power, has just started to
supply electricity.
One of the conditions under which the power station
was allowed laid down that oil and not coal was to
be burned. Other conditions were that the building
was approved by the Royal Fine Arts Commission, and
that the building must be set back far enough from
the Thames not to interfere with the projected road
and promenade. The protests about the building
came from the London County Council, the City Council,
and the Southwark Council, from the Dean and
Chapter of St. Paul's Cathedral - the planned power
station was opposite to St. Paul's, on the other side
of the river - and from such bodies as the Society
for the Protection of Ancient Buildings. Opposition
became so strong that in January 1947 a public
inquiry was held. The Government, however, allowed
the building, provided that the conditions were
observed.
When completed the station will comprise four
60,000-kilowatt generating sets, when the oil
consumption at full load, 16-hours a day, will be 67
tons an hour, consuming (in one winter's day) about
850 tons.
January 20th. 1953. PN-h.

204358      GAI
'FISHY STORY' FOR THE AMERICANS?
UNITED STATES TO BE 'INVADED' BY KIPPERS.
London:   Kipper connoisseurs from both sides of
the Atlantic turned up at Claridges Hotel here for
a Kipper Breakfast - held to celebrate the
'launching' of Scots kippers on the American
housewife.  Hosts at the breakfast - succulent,
juicy Scots kippers took the 'plate' of honour -
were Sir Frederick Bell, chairman of the Herring
Industry Board, and Lady Bell.
To introduce the Kipper 'in all its proud glory'
to America, four million Scots kippers are now on
their way in refrigerated boats to New York. The
invasion is due to open up in New York and New
England within the next few days.
Said Sir Frederick: "The majority of kippers sold
in America are not Scottish, and these, we think,
cannot compare with the genuine Highland article".

Professor Denis Brogan (a well-known Transatlantic
broadcaster, an authority on the American way of
life - and a kipper connoisseur) are served with
kippers at the breakfast at Claridges Hotel, London.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY, AUGUST 16th.
THE PROGRESS OF A NEW TOWN
JS  16.8.50.
HARLOW is one of eight New Towns, designed for the reception of
population and industry from the crowded areas of inner London,
and which are expected to take about 250,000 Londoners. Harlow's
contribution to this being an increase in population of 55,000.
HARLOW recently reached a distinct stage in its development with
the commencement of building work in the MARK HALL area - a step
which marked the beginning of work on the New Town proper and
the end of preparation which has lasted since the approval of
the Master Plan. This Plan was the first to receive official
approval despite the fact that the Corporation was by no means the
first to be set up. Much work has also been done in the CHIPPINGFIELD
area, where terraced and semi-detached houses have been erected,
and some of which are already in occupation by members of the
Corporation's staff and employees of the contractors. This recent
series of pictures gives some idea of the well-planned lay-out,
and the types of houses in course of erection.  Picture shows
the lounge of a 3-bedroomed terraced type house at CHIPPINGFIELD.
This house has a dining-kitchen and is let at an inclusive rent

as fencing, hurdles, tools and ladders. Fruit picking
ladders of special design is the speciality of the

MR. NUTT BUILDS A DREAM HOUSE
September 5th 1963 PAR 105014-1 (PNR/P-R)

MR. NUTT BUILDS A DREAM HOUSE

Seen here nearing completion is the nine-room
house being built at Keynsham, Somerset, for
himself and his family by 35-year-old Mr.
Raymond Nutt, who lives at present in a
Council house.
After spending two years on the foundations
and drainage, Mr. Nutt started to build last
Christmas and pressed on with the job despite
the Arctic winter.
He has carried out most of the work, doing it
in the evenings and at weekends when not at
his job on the maintenance staff of a Bristol
firm, but he has had help from his wife and
children (a girl and two boys aged 10, 8 and 6)
his two brothers and friends.
The house, a dormer bungalow built in
reconstructed Bath stone with timbered eaves,
will be a housewife's dream with 'all mod.
cons.' - full central heating (done by a
specialist firm), a playroom in the basement
for the children, a 'laundrette' off the
kitchen-diner and wash basins in the bedrooms.
Mr. Nutt reckons it will be worth £4,500.
September 5th 1963 PAR 105014-1 (PNR/P-R)

---
Sinfield June 61

TV cattle just
love cowboys

WHEN it's television time in the cowshed the farmer
switches on happily. For he claims that cow-
boys, cricket and commercials mean more milk in
the churns.
The farmer, 60-year-old
Charlie Pidgeon, says that
TV makes his cows more
contented — and there is
nothing like a contented cow
for giving those extra pints.
He explained yesterday:
"I've had the sets in the
milking shed for only four
days, but already there is a
difference of about two
gallons a day.
"Some sheds have sound
radio or long-playing equip-
ment. I have gone one better
and put in TV as a six-week
experiment.
"I shall carry on with it if
the increased milk yield con-
tinues."
Already the 25 "TV" cows
are reported to have their
own favourite programmes.
Freda Fillpail, a sturdy
Guernsey, watches absorbed
when a "Western" comes on.
Cartoon show
But her stallmates, Cider-
water and Dreamland Deidre,
seem to chew more happily
in their shed at Bosshill
Farm, Axmouth, Devon, when
watching a children's car-
toon show.
The farmer's wife, Mrs.
Ethel Pidgeon, explained
that the family are all TV
fans, and had one of the first
sets in Devon.
She said: "We have two
sets, one in the parlour and
the other in the living room.
And I believe the cows are
going to take to television,
too.
"In the days of hand milk-
ing I used to hum and say a
friendly word to the cows.
They like a bit of company."
And television brings the
cows plenty of company.
Children call at the cowshed
at milking time to join the
"viewers."

description: A photographic print from the Daily Herald Archive folder: Industry Â» Fuel + Power - Coal Â» Surface - Opencast.
gem_transcription_flat:

SUN.   WILLIAMS.     14-4-68.
A lucky strike left by motorway contractors after they had removed th
thousands of tons of soil, a seam of coal a yard thick for anyone
to pick. The scene was at Bently, Walsall near the new extention on
the M.6 motorway. Hundreds of Walsall towns people set to work
this weekend to take away all they could carry, by motorcar, van,
lorries, anything that would help them fill their coal sheds for
the winter, and all free.
---
COPYRIGHT
PHOTOGRAPH
by WILLIAMS
---
INDUS. COAL OPENCAST
---
IN STAFFORDSHIRE yesterday, it seemed that almost everybody was going out to get the coal in. With the difference that where they were getting the coal in from — if you follow — was not the coal bunker, but an actual coal mine handily sited by the side of the M6 at Bentley.
It was discovered, this deposit of what may nowadays be called Black Gold, by contractors excavating for motorway extensions. A fine seam of what experts describe as good quality coal, almost on the surface.
In much the same way as the news came from the Klondike, word soon got round.
In the Easter sunshine, they toiled ceaselessly, displaying an industry which in other circumstances would gladden Lord Robens's heart. Among them there was that cheerful camaraderie almost peculiar to those who are getting something for nothing, and there were complaints only about the enterprising chaps who brought along a mechanical digger. That, it was felt, was not playing the game.
Even the Coal Board seemed not too put out at this private enterprise competition. Their man, A. Spokeman, said amiably: "Strictly speaking, it all belongs to us. But it depends on how much is there."
Nevertheless, grub-stakers contemplating a quick dash up the M6 may rest assured that if the Staffordshire strike turns out to rival the Ruhr, then the bonanza will be pretty smartly ended.
In the Coal Rush, as it often was in the Klondike, the claim-jumpers are ready . . .
FREE COAL
---
BACK 1st
5 col x 6 1/2 deep
---
SUN
USED
15 APR 1968

"THE SPIDER MEN"
GO SLOW    DG/RS

Eleven thousand steel erectors - "the spider men" -
are starting to "go slow" on instructions from the
Constructional Engineering Union, this week. It is
estimated that this will slow up the rate of steel
frame building production by about 50%.
Called "spider men" because of their feats of skill
and balance high above the ground, on steel girders,
the steel erectors have the highest accident rate
in the building industry.
The "work-to-rule" movement, which means that every
safety regulation in the book will be religiously
carried out, follows the refusal of the Engineering
Employers' National Federation to grant an increase
of 3d an hour, with a rise in "height money".

PHOTO SHOWS: - "Coming down". Typical of the risks
run by the "spidermen" is this descent by means of the
jutting heads of rivets. "Spidermen" are JOCK BARRY
of Glasgow, and GERALD FLETCHER of Fulham. They
are working on a block of offices in Farringdon

---
1968
1243 Roll
---
IN THE tragedy of Ronan Point
yesterday, the only blessing was
that it happened too early to
become a full-scale disaster.

Too early. At 5.45 am., to be exact.
Too early for the families in the 22-
storey block of East End flats to be
up and busying themselves in their
sitting-rooms.

For, miraculously, it was 22 identical
living rooms which collapsed, in the
inevitable simile, "like a pack of cards."

In 22 identical bedrooms, families were
shocked, shattered, scared and totally be-
wildered. But, most of them, they escaped
the avalanche that thundered past their
bedroom doors.

'MATTER OF PROVIDENCE'

As Home Secretary Mr. James Callaghan
said on his tour of inspection: "It was
obviously a matter of providence that these
people were not in their living rooms."

A policeman was more blunt: "If it had
happened an hour later, the death roll
would have been very much higher," he said.

So, quite amazingly, the death roll was
infinitely less than anyone could have
hoped. And in nearby houses, and a school
where those who escaped gathered, as if still
seeking mutual protection, the survivors
wonderingly told the tales which will live
with them for the rest of their lives.

There was 56-year-old Miss Ivy Hodge, in
whose 18th floor kitchen it is believed the
collapse started. "I was putting the kettle
on," she said, "and the next moment I was
on the floor. There were flames everywhere
and I remember staggering to the door of
my flat so that someone could help me."

Somebody did. Miss Hodge was taken to
hospital and treated for burns.

There was Mr. James Chambers and his
wife Beatrice, aged 62, who were asleep in
their 7th floor flat. He said: "Suddenly our
bedroom wall fell away with a terrible rip-
ping sound. And we found ourselves staring
out over London...

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS 22.1.46.
BRITISH "HAND-MADE" CARS LEAD WORLD EXPORTS.
Beat industrial export news of the new year 1946 is that
Britain is giving the world a lead in motor car exports,
and that our plants are hard put to cope withthe demand
abroad for the small, high-performance economical designs
for which Britain has always been supreme.
Estmiatedoutput figures for this year are impressive,
including as they do 470,000 private cars, 136,000 load
carriers and 12,000 service vehicles. Incidentally, these
figures are higher than those for the peak production year
of 1938. Of these the Rootes Group will ship cars to 79
countries on orders valued at £7,500,000, whilst the Nuffield
Organisation's vast commitments include orders from India
alone worth £1,200,000.
The Government's request to the industry for an export
program target at least 50% greater than before the war
means that their value must exceed £30,000,000 a year ; the
challenge has been gladly accepted.
The accompanying photos were taken at two of the Rootes
Group's London factories, and are designed to show the
British "hand-made" craftmanship which is our promising
answer to the mass-production conveyer-belt methods of other
car production countries.
The picture shows
S.1 General view in the finishing shop at Thrupp &
Maberley's where bodies for the famous Humber
are made
